clue.text: King (not Henry) takes most of the bedspread from 2

indicators.note: not Henry tells us to drop the letter standing for Henry from the king's name

parts.note: John is a king's name, as in King John of England
H is a standard abbreviation for Henry, the unit of inductance

indicators.note: most of a word means all but its final letter is kept here

parts.note: a quilt is a bedspread

explanation.surface: A king named John, minus a letter, steals most of the covers from the bed of 2.
explanation.walkthrough: '2' refers to the answer at 2-down, NARCISSUS; 'from' is a link. 'not Henry' drops H from JOHN, and 'most of' trims QUILT to QUIL.
explanation.definitionFit: The jonquil is one species within the narcissus genus of spring bulbs, so it is an example of the flower.

clue.text: Man lifted first prize

parts.note: jack is a word for a man, as in every man jack

indicators.note: lifted in a down clue means the word is read upwards, backwards

parts.note: top means first, as in top of the class

explanation.surface: A man has stolen the first prize.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lifted' suggests theft; in a down clue it turns TOP upwards into POT.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackpot is the largest prize in a lottery or game.

clue.text: The epitome of egotism found in bed

explanation.surface: The most self-absorbed person is always lying in bed.
explanation.walkthrough: The bed is a flowerbed, not a sleeper's bed.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth, the youth who fell in love with his own reflection is the type of vanity; the same name is a spring flower grown in garden beds.

clue.text: Change a little money in America and in France

indicators.note: in means the money goes inside the abbreviation for America

parts.note: US is the United States of America
P, a penny, is a little money
et is the French for and

explanation.surface: A small coin swapped in the United States and in France.
explanation.definitionFit: To upset something is to disturb or alter it, to throw it into a changed state.

clue.text: English captain diverted from Luton, then?

indicators.note: diverted suggests the letters of Luton then are sent off on a new route

explanation.surface: An England skipper has been rerouted away from Luton, perhaps by an airline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from' is a link. Len Hutton captained England's cricket team in the 1950s; Luton is an English town with an airport.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Len Hutton was the Yorkshire batsman who captained England's Test cricket side, regaining the Ashes in 1953.

clue.text: Copy of admonition

parts.note: a repro is a reproduction, a copy

explanation.surface: A duplicate of a formal warning.
explanation.definitionFit: A reproof is a rebuke or scolding, the same thing as an admonition.

clue.text: Finally painting (in red) the town

indicators.note: in places the final letter of painting inside the colour

parts.note: ruby is a deep red

indicators.note: finally means the last letter of painting

explanation.surface: At last, out painting the town red.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface plays on painting the town red; the town is the answer itself, the Warwickshire market town where the game was born.
explanation.definitionFit: Rugby is a market town in Warwickshire, England, famous for its school.

clue.text: Tommy King, commander of a belligerent vessel

parts.note: Tommy is slang for a British private soldier
ER, Edward Rex, stands for a king

explanation.surface: A soldier called Tommy King is captain of a warship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tommy' looks like a first name; Tommy Atkins was the nickname for a British private.
explanation.definitionFit: A privateer was a privately owned armed ship licensed for war against enemy shipping, and also the person commanding it.

clue.text: Mature doctor turned up in the end

indicators.note: turned up in a down clue means the paired pieces are read upwards, backwards

parts.note: to age is to mature
MO, medical officer, is a doctor

explanation.surface: An older doctor arrived at last.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned up' reads like arrived; it reverses AGE plus MO. 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet, so it stands for the finish of anything.

clue.text: Qualified people ultimately get appointment

parts.note: fit means qualified or suitable
men are people

indicators.note: ultimately means the last letter of get

explanation.surface: Qualified candidates eventually land the job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'appointment' suggests a job but means a fitting, as in the appointments of a room.
explanation.definitionFit: A fitment is a piece of fixed furniture or equipment, and appointments are a building's fixtures and fittings.

clue.text: A body of men, but not the entire body

indicators.note: not the entire word is used, so its last letter is cut away

parts.note: a corpse is a dead body

explanation.surface: A group of men that is somehow less than a whole person.
explanation.walkthrough: The second 'body' is a dead one, CORPSE; lose its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A corps is an organised military unit or group of people working together.

clue.text: In undress, nudist outwardly disregarding fashion

parts.note: undress in the old sense of informal or partial clothing; négligé is a variant spelling of negligee, a light dressing gown

indicators.note: outwardly means only the outside letters of nudist are taken

explanation.surface: A nudist, half-clothed and wholly unconcerned about the latest styles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' is a link. NEGLIGE uses the accented spelling négligé, without the final E of negligee, and is followed by NT, the first and last letters of 'nudist'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being negligent means being careless and inattentive, here careless about one's appearance and dress.

clue.text: Tidy-up — not unusual chore for policeman

indicators.note: unusual signals that the letters of tidy-up and not are arranged in an unusual order

explanation.surface: Tidying up is an ordinary household task for a constable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unusual' rearranges TIDYUP plus NOT. Point duty is the British term for a police officer standing at a junction directing traffic.
explanation.definitionFit: Point duty is a police officer's posting at a fixed spot to direct traffic, a routine job for a constable.

clue.text: Saw in illustration woman's back

parts.note: Ada is a woman's name

indicators.note: back signals the abbreviation for an illustration is read backwards

parts.note: EG, for example, introduces an illustration

explanation.surface: Spotted in a picture: a woman's back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Saw' looks like the past of 'see' but is a noun, a saying; 'in' is a link, and 'back' turns the illustration's abbreviation round after the woman's name.
explanation.definitionFit: A saw is an old proverb or maxim, a traditional saying.

clue.text: Experience state can provide

indicators.note: the letters of state can provide another word when they are rearranged

explanation.surface: A state of mind is something a person can live through.
explanation.definitionFit: To taste something is to experience it, as in having a taste of freedom.

clue.text: Working women tend to find source of permanent income

indicators.note: working suggests the letters of women tend are being worked into a new shape

explanation.surface: Employed women generally build up a lasting income.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to find' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: An endowment is a fund given to an institution whose investment yields a steady, lasting revenue.

clue.text: Office location about to become highly confidential

indicators.note: about tells us the whole pairing of office and location runs backwards

parts.note: terce is a church office, the service said at the third hour of the day
a spot is a location

explanation.surface: Something in a particular office is about to be classified.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' reverses TERCE plus SPOT to give TOPS + ECRET. 'to become' is a link. 'Office' is not a workplace but a church service.
explanation.definitionFit: Top secret is the highest classification for government information that must stay private.

clue.text: Eric's alternative for a buffet?

explanation.surface: What Eric would choose instead of a buffet meal.
explanation.walkthrough: Dean Farrar's Victorian school story is titled 'Eric, or, Little by Little', so its alternative title means bit by bit. A buffet is a meal of pieces. 'for' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Piecemeal means gradually, bit by bit, the alternative title of the novel Eric; read as two words it is a meal of separate pieces, like a buffet.

clue.text: Rearranged e-g. central figure

indicators.note: rearranged tells us the letters of the example abbreviation and central are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A figure placed centrally, for example, after some reshuffling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'figure' is the definition, a geometric shape, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: A rectangle is a four-sided geometric shape with right angles.

clue.text: Home team held in abhorrence after the first half

indicators.note: held in means one piece is placed inside the other
only what comes after the first half of abhorrence is used, its final five letters

parts.note: a side is a team in sport

explanation.surface: Fans of the home team are held in contempt by everyone else.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Home' looks like it belongs with 'team' as in home side, but it is the definition; the team is the piece held inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A residence is a dwelling, the place where someone lives.

clue.text: Badger's home in animal's favour

indicators.note: in places the badger's home inside the animal

parts.note: a roe is a small deer, an animal
a sett is a badger's burrow

explanation.surface: A badger's lair is seen kindly by some animal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'favour' is a ribbon badge, not kindness.
explanation.definitionFit: A favour is a ribbon or badge worn as a token of support, which a rosette is.

clue.text: Bird circles cricket club looking for enemies

indicators.note: circles means the bird's letters go round the club's

parts.note: a ree is the female of the ruff, a wading bird, also called a reeve

explanation.surface: A bird of prey hovers over a cricket ground searching for rivals.
explanation.walkthrough: REE is a crossword favourite for a female ruff.
explanation.definitionFit: A recce, short for reconnaissance, is a scouting mission to look over enemy positions.

clue.text: Incessant scraps in which the French may be seen participating

indicators.note: in which ... participating means the French article is placed among the letters of scraps

parts.note: ends are scraps or leftovers, as in odds and ends
les is French for the, plural

explanation.surface: Constant fights involving the French.
explanation.walkthrough: 'scraps' looks like fights but means leftovers, ENDS.
explanation.definitionFit: Endless means going on without stopping, which is what incessant describes.

clue.text: Pay a shilling to working men

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for a shilling, the old British coin worth twelve pence
a crew is a team of men working together

explanation.surface: Hand over a shilling to the labourers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a' and 'to' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: Screw is old slang for wages or salary, as in being on a good screw.

clue.text: 5 ac leads doctor a dance

parts.note: the cross-reference points to rugby, the game at 5 down, whose usual abbreviation for rugby union is RU
MB, Bachelor of Medicine, is a doctor

explanation.surface: The answer at 5 leads a doctor into a dance.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference is printed as 5 across but must mean 5 down, RUGBY, abbreviated RU. 'leads' is a link putting it first.
explanation.definitionFit: The rumba is a ballroom dance of Cuban origin.

clue.text: Hull's visible side not regulated by council

parts.note: free means not regulated, as in a free market
a board is a council or governing committee

explanation.surface: In the city of Hull, the side that is open to view has escaped the council's control.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hull' suggests the English city but is the body of a ship. 'by' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Freeboard is the part of a ship's side between the waterline and the deck, visible above the water.

clue.text: Money — Anatole's a bit short

indicators.note: a bit short means the final letter of the name is dropped

parts.note: Anatole France was the French novelist

explanation.surface: Anatole is running low on cash.
explanation.walkthrough: Anatole France won the 1921 Nobel Prize for Literature; trim the last letter of his surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The franc was the currency of France and is still that of Switzerland.

clue.text: Dim member of invincible army

indicators.note: member of means a part of the words invincible army is taken

explanation.surface: A slow-witted soldier in an unbeatable army.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dim' looks like stupid but means blurred.
explanation.definitionFit: Blear means blurred or misty, as eyes are when dim with tears or tiredness.

clue.text: Paddy, the crew say, is abstemious

parts.note: a paddy is a fit of temper

indicators.note: say signals that the word for the crew is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: an eight is a rowing crew of eight oarsmen

explanation.surface: Paddy, according to his rowing crew, does not drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Paddy' looks like an Irishman's name but is a tantrum.
explanation.definitionFit: Temperate means moderate in drinking and eating, which is what abstemious describes.

clue.text: Standard? This is much better than that

definitions.text: This is much better than that

explanation.surface: A note asking whether one thing far outclasses the usual.
explanation.walkthrough: A Roman legion's standard was topped by an eagle. In golf, par is the standard score and an eagle is two strokes under it.
explanation.definitionFit: A Roman army's banner bore the bird's figure; in golf, a hole played two strokes under par is far better than par, the standard.

clue.text: Supple eastern holy man lay around

indicators.note: around means the word for lay goes round the holy man

parts.note: laic means lay, not of the clergy
ST, for saint, is a holy man

explanation.surface: A flexible Eastern holy man lounged about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lay' looks like a verb but is an adjective, LAIC.
explanation.definitionFit: Elastic means flexible and springy, just as supple does.

clue.text: 'Bounty' a tidy ship

parts.note: tidy can mean considerable or large, as in a tidy sum
SS, for steamship, is a ship

explanation.surface: The Bounty described as a neat vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bounty' suggests the famous ship, but is generosity; 'tidy' is not neat but large.
explanation.definitionFit: Largess is generous giving, a gift handed out freely, which is what bounty means.
